```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.8)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")
```

## A chart maps columns to visual properties

```{r}
#| label: template
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = column1, y = column2), data = my_tibble)
```

- `ggplot()`: an empty chart. `+` adds layers.
- `geom_*()`: the **geometry** that draws the data: points, lines, bars.
- `aes()`: **mappings** from columns to visual properties: x, y, colour, size, fill.
- `data =`: the tibble to plot. Name it: a `geom_*()` takes the mapping first.

::: {.notes}
- Swapping the order, `geom_point(by_aa, aes(...))`, fails with "`mapping` must be created by `aes()`. ✖ You've supplied a data frame."
:::

## Summarise first, then plot

```{r}
#| label: by-aa
by_aa <- bca |>
  filter(!is.na(aa_label)) |>
  group_by(aa_label) |>
  summarise(avg_floorarea = mean(floorarea, na.rm = TRUE),
            avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())
by_aa |> head(4)
```

## geom_point() shows a relationship

```{r}
#| label: point
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(avg_floorarea, avg_price), data = by_aa)
```

## Map more columns to colour and size

```{r}
#| label: colour-size
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(avg_floorarea, avg_price, colour = aa_label, size = n),
             data = by_aa)
```

## Mapping and setting are different

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: mapped
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(avg_floorarea, avg_price,
        colour = "blue"),
    data = by_aa)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: set
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(avg_floorarea, avg_price),
    colour = "blue",
    data = by_aa)
```
:::
::::

Inside `aes()`, `"blue"` is treated as data. Outside `aes()`, it sets the colour.

## Layers stack: lines and points

```{r}
#| label: lines
#| fig-height: 2.4
avg_price <- bca |>
  group_by(act_use_cat, sale_year = year(sale_date)) |>
  summarise(avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price) +
  geom_point(aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat), data = avg_price)
```

Each layer has its own mapping and data, so we write both twice.

## Global and local mappings

```{r}
#| label: global
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(avg_price, aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

The same chart as the last slide. Data and `aes()` in `ggplot()` are **global**: every layer uses them, so you write them once. `aes()` in a `geom_*()`, as on the last slide, is **local**: only that layer uses it.

::: {.notes}
- `ggplot()` takes the data first; a `geom_*()` takes the mapping first. A layer usually reuses the plot's data but needs its own mapping.
- Data first in `ggplot()` also lets you pipe into it: `van17 |> count(act_use_cat) |> ggplot(aes(n, act_use_cat))`.
:::

## geom_line() joins the points within each group

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: local
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: group
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.8
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = act_use_cat))
```
:::
::::

Left: with no groups, the line joins every point in year order. Right: `group` splits the line, as `group_by()` splits rows. On the last slide, `colour` did the same: a text column in `colour` also sets the group.

::: {.notes}
- A numeric column in `colour` does not set the group, so it does not split the line.
- ggplot2 groups by every discrete column mapped in the layer: `colour`, `fill`, `linetype`, `shape`, and `group`.
:::

## A smaller dataset: Vancouver in 2017

```{r}
#| label: van17
van17 <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) == 2017) |>
  mutate(price_m = price / 1e6)
nrow(van17)
```

The next charts use `van17`: one city in one year, so the points do not pile up. `price_m` is the price in millions of dollars.

## Quick check: how many fitted lines?

```{r}
#| label: quiz-local
#| eval: false
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = act_use_cat), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

**A.** One  **B.** Two, one for each property type

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: quiz-local-answer
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = act_use_cat), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

**A.** `colour` is local to `geom_point()`, so `geom_smooth()` has one group and fits one line to all the points. Move `colour` into `ggplot()` to get one line per type.
:::

## Choose the geometry for the question

| Question | Geometry |
|---|---|
| How are two numbers related? | `geom_point()` |
| How does a value change over time? | `geom_line()` |
| How do groups compare? | `geom_col()` for values you computed, `geom_bar()` to count rows |
| How is one number distributed? | `geom_histogram()` |

## geom_bar() counts for you; geom_col() does not

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: bar-count
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
ggplot(van17, aes(y = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_bar()
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: col-count
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
van17 |>
  count(act_use_cat) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, act_use_cat)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
::::

The same chart. `geom_bar()` counts the rows itself, so its axis says `count`, a column it computed. `geom_col()` draws the `n` you computed.

## Some geoms compute what they draw

| Geom | Computes before drawing |
|---|---|
| `geom_bar()` | The number of rows in each group |
| `geom_histogram()` | Bins, then the number of rows in each bin |
| `geom_smooth()` | A fitted line, as in the quick check |
| `geom_boxplot()` | The median and quartiles |
| `geom_col()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_line()` | Nothing: they draw the values as given |

::: {.key-point}
When a geom computes, ask what it computed. `geom_bar()` counts rows, not people (deck 07).
:::

::: {.notes}
- `geom_bar(stat = "identity")` is the same as `geom_col()`. AI-written and older code often uses it.
- `after_stat(count)`, or the older `..count..`, refers to a column the geom computed.
- `geom_bar(aes(x, y))` fails with "`stat_count()` must only have an x or y aesthetic": `geom_bar()` computes y itself.
:::

## Look up what a geom draws

| Resource | Use it to |
|---|---|
| [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) ([PDF](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf)) | See every geom as a small picture |
| [ggplot2 reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/) | Read one function's arguments and example charts |
| [R Graph Gallery](https://r-graph-gallery.com/) | Find a chart type and see working code |
| [From Data to Viz](https://www.data-to-viz.com/) | Choose a chart from the kind of data you have |

In Positron, `?geom_histogram` opens the help page, and `example(geom_histogram)` draws its examples.

**Try it:** pick a geom from the cheat sheet that we have not used, read its page, and draw it with `van17`.

## scale_*() turns values into axes and colours

The name says what changes: `scale_`, the mapping, then how.

::: {.small}
| Function | Changes |
|---|---|
| `scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2000, 2010, 2020))` | Which x values get a gridline and a label |
| `scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000))` | The x-axis range, **dropping rows outside it** |
| `scale_x_log10()` | The x-axis, to a log scale |
| `scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2")` | The colours for the `colour` mapping |
:::

::: {.key-point}
When you review AI-written code, you can skim most `scale_*()` lines: they change labels and colours. Stop at `limits`, which drops rows, and log scales, which change what geoms compute.
:::

## Axis limits can remove data

`van17` holds City of Vancouver sales in 2017, with `price_m` in millions.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: limits
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 2000)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5))
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: coord
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price_m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2000),
                  ylim = c(0, 5))
```
:::
:::
::::

Left: `limits` dropped the `r sum(van17$floorarea > 2000, na.rm = TRUE)` homes over 2,000 sq ft **before** fitting the line. Right: `coord_cartesian()` only zooms.

## Log scales spread out skewed data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: no-log
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: log
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
ggplot(van17, aes(floorarea, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar())
```
:::
:::
::::

Left: a few large, expensive homes stretch the axes, and most sales crowd into a corner. Right: on a log scale each gridline is a multiple of the last, so the spread shows.

`scales::label_dollar()` uses `label_dollar()` from the scales package without loading it. `label_comma()` and `label_percent()` work the same way.

::: {.notes}
- `label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")` writes 2,000,000 as 2M. Decks 07 and 10 use it.
- A log scale transforms the data before geoms compute. `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` on these axes fits log price on log floor area, a different line from the one on the original axes.
:::

## The functions around the geoms

::: {.small}
| Family | Controls | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `scale_*()` | How values become axes and colours: limits, breaks, number formats, log scales | `scale_y_log10()` |
| `coord_*()` | The plotting area: zoom, flip | `coord_flip()` |
| `facet_*()` | One panel per group | `facet_wrap(~ act_use_cat)` |
| `labs()` | Text: title, axis names, legend title, caption | `labs(y = "Price")` |
| `theme_*()`, `theme()` | The look that is not data: background, fonts, legend position | `theme_minimal()` |
| `guides()` | Legends | `guides(colour = "none")` |
:::

Inside a geom, `alpha`, `linewidth`, and `position = "dodge"` set that layer's look. Use these names when you ask AI to restyle a chart; to sort bars by value, ask for `fct_reorder()`.

## Read a long AI-written chart

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: ai-chart
#| eval: false
# 1. data and mappings
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  # 2. what to draw
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  # 3. how values become labels and colours
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  # 4. text
  labs(title = "Average sale price",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  # 5. the look that is not data
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| label: ai-chart-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(avg_price,
       aes(sale_year, avg_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(title = "Average sale price",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
::::

::: {.key-point}
Only `ggplot()`, `aes()`, and `geom_*()` decide what is drawn. The rest changes how it looks, except `limits`, which drops rows, and log scales, which change what geoms like `geom_smooth()` compute.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Order matters for themes: `theme(legend.position = "bottom") + theme_minimal()` silently resets the legend, because a complete theme replaces earlier `theme()` settings. Put `theme_minimal()` first.
- To learn what a line does, comment it out and run the chart again.
:::

## Practice: price trends by property type

For the City of Vancouver, plot the median sale price in each year from 2000 to 2025, with one line for each `act_use_cat`.

1. Summarise first: one row per year and property type.
2. Map `act_use_cat` to `colour`.
3. Show the prices in dollars on the y-axis.

## Answer

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: trend-practice
#| fig-height: 3
van_trend <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", year(sale_date) <= 2025) |>
  group_by(year = year(sale_date), act_use_cat) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

trend_plot <- ggplot(van_trend, aes(year, median_price, colour = act_use_cat)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
trend_plot
```
:::

## Save a chart for your slides

```{r}
#| label: save
#| eval: false
ggsave("temp/van_trend.png", trend_plot, width = 8, height = 4.5)
```

::: {.key-point}
Save the chart in an object, then pass it to `ggsave()`. Use the PNG in PowerPoint or Google Slides.
:::
